column1: LPN vs RN — what can an LPN NOT do?
column2: Cannot do independent assessment. Cannot give IV push medications. Cannot diagnose. Cannot independently plan care. Must work under RN or MD supervision at all times.

column1: ADN vs BSN — what is the difference?
column2: ADN = 2-year RN degree. BSN = 4-year RN degree with broader competencies in research / leadership / community health / policy / QI.

column1: DNP vs PhD in nursing — what is the difference?
column2: DNP = Doctor of Nursing Practice (clinical practice degree). PhD = Doctor of Philosophy in Nursing (research degree).

column1: Who gives the NCLEX and what does passing mean?
column2: Given by NCSBN. Passing = minimum competency — NOT excellence.

column1: Do ADN and BSN students take the same NCLEX?
column2: Yes — both take the NCLEX-RN.

column1: What happens when a patient on warfarin eats large amounts of leafy greens?
column2: Leafy greens are high in Vitamin K, which reduces warfarin effectiveness and lowers INR — increasing clotting risk.

column1: Who can issue a nursing license?
column2: Only the state BON (Board of Nursing).

column1: What must be disclosed when applying for or renewing a nursing license?
column2: Criminal history / substance misuse within last 5 years / any disciplinary actions against a professional license

column1: What are the 4 APRN roles?
column2: CRNA (Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetist) / CNM (Certified Nurse-Midwife) / CNS (Clinical Nurse Specialist) / NP (Nurse Practitioner)

column1: Benner's 5 stages of nursing development in order?
column2: Novice → Advanced Beginner → Competent → Proficient → Expert

column1: Novice vs Advanced Beginner nurse — how do they differ?
column2: Novice = no experience / cannot draw on own judgment. Advanced Beginner = recognizes patterns / focuses on following rules / needs clinical support for priorities.

column1: Competent vs Proficient vs Expert nurse — how do they differ?
column2: Competent = prioritizes from past experience / mastery in multiple areas. Proficient = understands bigger picture / modifies plans when situations change. Expert = trusts intuition / self-confidence / knows what needs to be done.

column1: Case Manager vs Change Agent nursing role — what is the difference?
column2: Case Manager = coordinates services / discharge planning / manages costs. Change Agent = advocates for changes needed to improve patient care / helps educate and facilitate change.

column1: What are the 6 QSEN competencies?
column2: Patient-Centered Care / Teamwork and Collaboration / Evidence-Based Practice / Quality Improvement / Safety / Informatics

column1: ANA vs NLN vs National Academy of Medicine — what does each do?
column2: ANA = enhances nursing profession / lobbies / publishes Code of Ethics. NLN = promotes nursing education / addresses educator shortage. National Academy of Medicine (formerly IOM) = uses EBP approach to improve global health.

column1: Signs of impaired nursing (SUD) — what to look for?
column2: Disheveled appearance / mood swings / isolation / rarely calls in sick (hospital = drug source) / frequently volunteers to give pain medications (possible diversion). MUST report immediately.

column1: What is the IOM Future of Nursing Report goal?
column2: 80% of nurses to have a BSN by 2020.

column1: What defines a Nurse Practice Act?
column2: Created by each individual STATE. Establishes definitions / rules / regulations for licensed nurses. Differs state to state.

column1: RN process vs LPN process — what is the difference?
column2: RN = 5 steps (ADPIE — full assessment). LPN = 4 steps (data collection / collaborative planning / implementation under supervision / evaluation with RN). LPN CANNOT do independent assessment.

column1: What CAN an LPN do?
column2: Vital signs / insert Foley catheters and NG tubes / wound care / give most medications (NOT IV push). Must work under RN or MD at all times.

column1: When must discharge planning begin?
column2: On ADMISSION — not at discharge.

column1: What does medication reconciliation involve and when does it occur?
column2: Creating accurate list of all medications (name / dosage / frequency / route) and comparing against orders. Occurs at ADMISSION / DISCHARGE / and TRANSFER.

column1: Where do most medication errors occur?
column2: During PRESCRIBING.

column1: What must you do with a verbal order?
column2: READ BACK — not just repeat — to verify it was correctly heard AND correctly transcribed.

column1: Lateral violence vs vertical violence — what is the difference?
column2: Lateral = peer-to-peer incivility (horizontal violence). Vertical = supervisor to employee or vice versa.

column1: Incivility vs bullying — what is the difference?
column2: Incivility = gossiping / being rude / refusing to help / interrupting. Bullying = incivility that is REPEATED — recurring harmful behavior.

column1: What are the 5 conflict management approaches and which is the goal?
column2: Dominate / Oblige / Avoid / Compromise / Integrate. Goal = COMPROMISE and INTEGRATE.

column1: What is I-SBAR-R?
column2: I=Introductions / S=Situation / B=Background / A=Assessment / R=Recommendation / R=Read back. Standard healthcare communication tool.

column1: Where should handoff report occur?
column2: At the BEDSIDE.

column1: What are the EBP steps in order?
column2: 1. Identify problem (PICOT) 2. Search credible sources 3. Evaluate findings 4. Implement recommendations 5. Review effectiveness 6. Disseminate results

column1: What does PICOT stand for?
column2: Population / Intervention / Comparison / Outcome / Time

column1: Peer-reviewed vs non-peer-reviewed — which is credible for EBP?
column2: Peer-reviewed = reviewed by professionals before publication = scholarly evidence. Non-peer-reviewed (newspapers/magazines) = NOT reliable for EBP.

column1: Quantitative vs qualitative research — what is the difference?
column2: Quantitative = numerical data / statistics / compares intervention vs control group. Qualitative = narrative data / explores experiences and feelings from participant perspective.

column1: What are the 3 elements of critical appraisal?
column2: Validity (did researchers conduct the study well?) / Reliability (can others reproduce results?) / Applicability (is the population similar to yours?)

column1: What is clinical judgment?
column2: The observed outcome of critical thinking and decision making — uses nursing knowledge to observe situations / identify prioritized concerns / generate evidence-based solutions. Gets better with experience.

column1: Critical thinking vs clinical reasoning — what is the difference?
column2: Critical thinking = uses logic / considers alternative approaches. Clinical reasoning = mental process used when analyzing ALL data in a clinical situation. Clinical judgment = clinical reasoning repeated over time.

column1: What are the 5 steps of ADPIE?
column2: Assessment → Analysis → Planning → Implementation → Evaluation

column1: Subjective vs objective data — what is the difference?
column2: Subjective = what patient REPORTS (pain/nausea/dizziness — patient must tell you). Objective = what you can OBSERVE or MEASURE (vital signs/vomiting/wound appearance). Example: nausea = subjective; vomiting = objective.

column1: Which clients must the RN personally assess?
column2: NEW clients AND UNSTABLE clients — cannot delegate initial assessment to LPN.

column1: What is PES format and when is it used?
column2: Problem + Etiology + Signs/Symptoms — used ONLY for ACTUAL problems currently happening.

column1: What does the etiology of a nursing diagnosis determine?
column2: The INTERVENTIONS — interventions must address the etiology not just the problem.

column1: What are SMART goals?
column2: Specific / Measurable / Attainable / Realistic / Timely

column1: What is the rule about making a care plan?
column2: NEVER make a plan of care without consulting the patient.

column1: What are the 5 rights of delegation?
column2: Right task / Right circumstance (stable client) / Right person / Right directions and communication / Right supervision and evaluation

column1: Who maintains accountability after delegating a task?
column2: The DELEGATOR (the nurse who delegated) — always maintains responsibility even after delegating.

column1: Can clinical reasoning be delegated to AP (assistive personnel)?
column2: NO — clinical reasoning can NEVER be delegated to AP/UAP.

column1: Direct care vs indirect care interventions — what is the difference?
column2: Direct = performed WITH the patient (giving meds / vital signs / physical care). Indirect = performed AWAY from patient (documentation / referrals).

column1: Independent vs dependent interventions — what is the difference?
column2: Independent = nurse performs WITHOUT a provider order. Dependent = REQUIRES a provider order.

column1: Maslow's hierarchy — what is the nursing priority order?
column2: 1. Physiological (food/water/air/shelter/sleep) — ALWAYS first 2. Safety and Security 3. Love and Belonging 4. Self-Esteem 5. Self-Actualization

column1: What does ABCDE stand for in priority setting?
column2: Airway → Breathing → Circulation → Disability (neurologic status) → Exposure (head-to-toe assessment)

column1: Triage tag colors and priority order?
column2: Red = life-threatening but survivable (FIRST priority) / Yellow = urgent (second) / Green = walking wounded (third) / Black = deceased or unsurvivable (lowest)

column1: Acute vs chronic — which gets priority and why?
column2: ACUTE over chronic — acute has less opportunity for physical adaptation.

column1: Unstable vs stable — which gets priority and examples of each?
column2: Unstable takes priority. Unstable = acute change in condition (uncontrolled bleeding / severe respiratory distress / frequently changing BP). Stable = condition changes little over time.

column1: What is the least restrictive/least invasive framework?
column2: Choose the intervention that maintains client safety while producing the LEAST amount of restriction or invasion. Applies to restraints too — choose one allowing as much movement as possible.

column1: What is the survival potential framework and when is it used?
column2: Prioritize clients with the greatest chance of survival when resources are LIMITED. Used in mass casualty/disaster triage.

column1: Critical vs urgent vs routine vs extra client care needs?
column2: Critical = intervene immediately (respiratory difficulty / chest pain / neuro change). Urgent = mild harm if delayed (post-op pain). Routine = routine meds/vitals. Extra = promotes comfort (warm blanket).

column1: Full-length siderails vs half-length siderails — which is a restraint?
column2: Full-length = RESTRAINT (prevents patient from getting out of bed). Half/quarter = NOT a restraint if patient can still exit bed independently.

column1: Tachycardia vs bradycardia — what are the values?
column2: Tachycardia = pulse OVER 100 bpm. Bradycardia = pulse UNDER 60 bpm.

column1: Tachypnea vs bradypnea — what are the values?
column2: Tachypnea = respiratory rate OVER 20. Bradypnea = respiratory rate UNDER 12.

column1: Normal temperature / respiratory rate / blood pressure?
column2: Temperature = 96.8–100.4°F. Respiratory rate = 12–20. Blood pressure = 120/80.

column1: What does Autonomy mean as an ethical principle?
column2: Respecting the patient's right to make their own healthcare decisions, including the right to refuse care.

column1: What does Veracity mean?
column2: Provide truthful and accurate information to the client at all times.

column1: What does Fidelity mean?
column2: Keep promises and uphold commitments to the client.

column1: What does Justice mean?
column2: Impartial, fair, equitable care regardless of age, sex, race, or economic status.

column1: What are the ANA nursing values (5)?
column2: Altruism / Human Dignity / Integrity / Autonomy / Social Justice

column1: What are the 8 ethical decision-making steps?
column2: 1. Is there a dilemma? 2. Define it 3. Identify solutions 4. Apply ethical principles 5. Include all stakeholders 6. Decide 7. Review 8. Act

column1: Under EMTALA what must happen before transferring a patient?
column2: Hospital must stabilize first. If unable to stabilize, the physician must sign off that the benefits of transfer outweigh the risks.

column1: HIPAA — what are the exceptions when confidentiality CAN be broken?
column2: Cases of ABUSE reporting / COMMUNICABLE DISEASE reporting.

column1: HIPAA violations — what are the consequences?
column2: Termination / fines / loss of nursing license / exposure to litigation / possible prison sentence.

column1: What is the nurse's role in informed consent?
column2: VERIFY and WITNESS the signature — the nurse does NOT obtain consent. Verify the patient has adequate knowledge to decide.

column1: Can a patient withdraw consent?
column2: Yes — at ANY time.

column1: Does a nurse need an attorney to witness an advance directive?
column2: No — a nurse can witness. No attorney needed. Federal law requires facilities to provide the forms.

column1: Malpractice vs negligence — what is the difference?
column2: Malpractice = fails to meet STANDARDS OF CARE. Negligence = breaches DUTY OF CARE resulting in client injury or suffering.

column1: What are nurses required to report as mandatory reporters?
column2: Maltreatment (physical/emotional/sexual/financial exploitation/educational neglect/denial of food or shelter). Communicable diseases (anthrax/botulism/chlamydia/hepatitis A-C/HIV/influenza/measles/TB/Zika).

column1: Incident report — is it part of the medical record and what should you NOT do?
column2: NOT part of the medical record — it is a risk management tool. NEVER reference the incident report in the medical chart.

column1: Just culture vs whistleblowing — what is the difference?
column2: Just culture = accountability without punishment / encourages reporting mistakes without fear. Whistleblowing = formally reporting illegal/unethical acts to a regulatory agency — consult BON and legal counsel FIRST.

column1: Trailing zeros vs leading zeros — what are the rules?
column2: Trailing zeros: AVOID — write 25 NOT 25.0 (could be read as 250). Leading zeros: ALWAYS USE — write 0.25 NOT .25 (could be read as 25).

column1: Medicaid vs Medicare — who do they cover?
column2: Medicaid = the POOR / low-income individuals. Medicare = the ELDERLY (65+) AND people with end-stage renal disease (dialysis patients).

column1: What is client abandonment?
column2: Deserting a client for whom a nurse-client relationship has been established without ensuring continuation of care by another nurse.

column1: What is GINA?
column2: Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (2008) — protects from discrimination based on genetic testing results.

column1: Braden Scale score ranges and risk levels?
column2: 19-23 = no risk / 15-18 = mild / 13-14 = moderate / 10-12 = high / 9 or less = very high risk

column1: Hendrich II vs Braden Scale — what does each measure and which direction is risk?
column2: Hendrich II = FALL RISK (higher score = higher risk). Braden = PRESSURE INJURY RISK (lower score = higher risk). Opposite directions.

column1: What are the 2 identifiers required for client identification?
column2: Name + date of birth OR medical record number. NEVER room number.

column1: What does RACE stand for in fire safety?
column2: Rescue (remove clients/visitors/employees) → Alarm (activate fire alarm) → Contain (close doors and windows — cuts oxygen to fire) → Extinguish (only if safe and proper extinguisher available)

column1: What causes alarm fatigue and why is it dangerous?
column2: Frequent false/nuisance alarms → staff become desensitized → may miss real emergencies or have slower response times.

column1: Do bed and chair alarms prevent falls?
column2: NO — they allow quick rescue if a patient gets up but do NOT prevent falls.

column1: Near miss vs adverse event vs sentinel event — what is the difference?
column2: Near miss = caught before reaching patient. Adverse event = actual harm occurred. Sentinel event = death / permanent injury / dismemberment / severe temporary harm.

column1: Pressure injury Stage 1 vs Stage 2 — how do they differ?
column2: Stage 1 = nonblanchable erythema of INTACT skin. Stage 2 = partial-thickness skin loss with EXPOSED DERMIS (shallow open wound / blister-like).

column1: What is an unstageable pressure injury?
column2: Full-thickness skin and tissue loss — base covered by slough or eschar / cannot determine true depth until removed.

column1: What is a Deep Tissue Pressure Injury (DTPI)?
column2: Persistent nonblanchable deep red / maroon / or purple discoloration of intact or non-intact skin — injury to underlying tissue.

column1: What are the risk factors for skin breakdown?
column2: Immobility / moisture / poor nutrition / friction and shear / sensory deficits

column1: Wound healing — primary vs secondary vs tertiary intention?
column2: Primary = edges sutured together (least scarring). Secondary = left open to heal from base up (more scarring). Tertiary = left open initially then sutured later (delayed closure).

column1: What is wound evisceration and how is it treated?
column2: Internal organs protrude through wound — EMERGENCY. Cover with sterile saline-moistened dressing and call provider immediately.

column1: What is chronic pain?
column2: Pain lasting longer than 6 months, constant or recurring, with no predictable end. Can be physically and emotionally debilitating.

column1: Nociceptive vs neuropathic pain — what is the difference?
column2: Nociceptive = pain in skin/bones/muscles/organs — localized / aching / stabbing / pounding. Neuropathic = nerve pain — burning / shooting / pins and needles / numbness (diabetic neuropathy / phantom limb).

column1: What does PQRST stand for in pain assessment?
column2: P=Precipitating cause / Q=Quality / R=Region / S=Severity (0-10) / T=Timing

column1: Numeric rating scale — what do the score ranges mean?
column2: 0 is no pain / 1-3 = mild / 4-6 = moderate / 7-10 = severe

column1: What is PCA and when is it used?
column2: Patient-Controlled Analgesia — patient presses a button to receive a small bolus at a basal rate as ordered. Used postoperatively.

column1: Opioids vs NSAIDs vs adjuvant analgesics — what is each used for?
column2: Opioids = strongest / most commonly prescribed for pain / can cause respiratory depression. NSAIDs = reduce inflammation/fever/pain — can cause bleeding. Adjuvant = help with neuropathic pain / reduce opioid dose needed.

column1: Every client has the right to what regarding pain?
column2: Pain management — regardless of the nurse's personal values. Undertreating pain violates beneficence and nonmaleficence.

column1: What are the 4 sleep stages and their key features?
column2: Stage 1 NREM = lightest / 5% of cycle. Stage 2 NREM = deeper / 50% of cycle / HR and temp decrease. Stage 3 NREM = deepest / delta waves / immune repair / tissue healing. Stage 4 REM = dreaming / muscles atonic / begins 90 min after falling asleep.

column1: What makes Stage 3 NREM sleep unique?
column2: Deepest sleep / immune system strengthens / muscles-tissues-bones repair / pulse and respirations at lowest. Older adults have FEWER Stage 3 cycles.

column1: What makes Stage 4 REM sleep unique?
column2: Dreaming stage / skeletal muscles atonic (protects from acting out dreams) / breathing irregular / elevated HR. Older adults have FEWER REM cycles.

column1: How many hours of sleep do adults need vs older adults?
column2: Adults (20-65) = 7-9 hours. Older adults (65+) = 7-8 hours. Older adults also have more Stage 2 cycles and fewer Stage 3 and REM cycles.

column1: Central sleep apnea vs obstructive sleep apnea — what is the difference?
column2: Central = brain fails to signal respiratory muscles → cessation of breathing (caused by opioid overdose or heart failure). Obstructive = upper airway physically collapses during sleep / snoring is common / treated with CPAP.

column1: What is narcolepsy and what is cataplexy?
column2: Narcolepsy = chronic sudden sleepiness / uncontrollable sleep attacks / difficulty staying awake. Cataplexy = brief loss of voluntary muscle tone triggered by emotion (laughter) — occurs with narcolepsy.

column1: What is the first-line sleep medication for older adults?
column2: Melatonin — non-habit forming / cost-effective / few side effects.

column1: Benzodiazepines for sleep — what is the concern?
column2: Can cause physical dependence — NOT recommended for long-term use. Use cautiously in older adults with decreased liver/kidney function.

column1: Simple vs complex carbohydrates — what is the difference?
column2: Simple = rapidly digested / quick glucose spike (white bread/sugar/candy/fruit juice). Complex = digested slowly / steady energy (whole grains/legumes/vegetables/brown rice).

column1: Why do vegan patients need B12 supplementation?
column2: B12 ONLY comes from animal sources — a vegan diet contains no B12.

column1: BMI categories — all 4 ranges?
column2: Under 18.5 = underweight / 18.5-24.9 = healthy / 25-29.9 = overweight / 30+ = obese

column1: Why avoid red-colored liquids for colon procedures or tonsillectomies?
column2: Can be confused with BLEEDING.

column1: Renal diet — what does it restrict and which foods are high potassium?
column2: Restricts sodium / potassium / phosphorus. High-potassium foods to AVOID: bananas/cantaloupe/tomatoes/oranges/prune juice/spinach/collard greens/kale/swiss chard.

column1: What supplement interactions are high yield for the exam?
column2: Vitamin K + warfarin = reduced warfarin effectiveness (increased clotting). St. John's Wort = decreases birth control/cardiac meds/antidepressants. Antioxidants (Vit C & E) = reduce chemotherapy effectiveness. Folic acid = reduces birth defect risk.

column1: What is the priority action if aspiration is suspected during tube feeding?
column2: STOP the tube feeding immediately. Do NOT lower HOB. Notify provider.

column1: What fever threshold indicates tube feeding aspiration?
NG vs NJ vs G-tube — who places each?
column2: NG = placed by NURSES at bedside. NJ = placed by PROVIDER using guided radiology / X-ray confirmation. G-tube = placed by SURGEON.

column1: NG vs NJ — what unique thing can only the NG do?
column2: NG ONLY — can remove stomach contents via suction. NJ bypasses the stomach and cannot remove stomach contents.

column1: How is NG tube placement verified?
column2: Initially by X-RAY before first use. Then every 4 hours by aspirating gastric contents and checking pH.

column1: Enteral feeding HOB rules?
column2: HOB 30-45° DURING tube feeding. HOB 30-45° for AT LEAST 1 HOUR after bolus feedings. Hold feedings when repositioning flat.

column1: What is gastric residual volume and what does >250 mL mean?
column2: Residual = undigested formula still sitting in the stomach, checked by aspirating the NG or G-tube with a syringe. >250 mL = stomach not emptying well → aspiration risk → follow facility policy.

column1: When is TPN used?
column2: When the GI tract cannot absorb or tolerate adequate nutrition. Nutrition is delivered intravenously into a large vein.

column1: What is the major complication of TPN?
column2: Hyperglycemia — monitor blood glucose frequently. Even non-diabetic patients may need insulin.

column1: Spinal curvatures — kyphosis vs scoliosis vs lordosis?
column2: Kyphosis = thoracic (upper back) — hunchback. Scoliosis = lateral S-shaped curve. Lordosis = lumbar (lower back) — swayback.

column1: Normal urinalysis values — list all.
column2: Color: pale yellow to amber / Specific gravity: 1.002-1.030 / Clarity: clear / Odor: mild / Protein: under 20 mg/dL / Glucose: negative / Ketones: negative / Hemoglobin: negative / Nitrite: negative / Leukocyte esterase: negative / Bacteria-yeast-parasites: none

column1: Minimum urine output for an adult?
column2: 30 mL/hour

column1: 6 types of urinary incontinence — what triggers each?
column2: Stress = coughing/sneezing/laughing/physical activity. Urge = strong urge but leaks before toilet (bladder training works). Reflex = nerve damage / no warning. Overflow = incomplete emptying / overfills. Functional = physical inability to reach toilet. Nocturnal enuresis = nighttime bedwetting.

column1: Stress vs urge incontinence — key difference for the exam?
column2: Stress = caused by PHYSICAL PRESSURE (coughing/sneezing/laughing). Urge = caused by OVERACTIVE BLADDER — strong urge but cannot make it. Bladder training works for URGE not stress.

column1: Foley catheter indications?
column2: Urinary retention / surgical procedures / wounds where urine contacts wound and prevents healing

column1: Clean catch urine culture — how is it collected?
column2: Wipe three times front-to-back → start urinating → stop → collect midstream. Ask about antibiotics first.

column1: 24-hour urine collection — how is it done?
column2: DISCARD first morning void. Collect ALL urine for next 24 hours. Keep refrigerated or on ice. Evaluates kidney function.

column1: FOBT — what does it detect and what causes false positives?
column2: Detects hidden blood in stool — turns BLUE if blood present. False positives: red meat / broccoli / beets / turnips / NSAIDs.

column1: Stool for ova and parasites — why must it go to lab immediately?
column2: Parasites die quickly and become difficult or impossible to identify.

column1: Fecal impaction — what is it and how is it treated?
column2: Hardened stool prevents evacuation. Treat with warm mineral oil enema → manual removal → surgery only if obstruction is complete.

column1: Diarrhea dietary risk factors — list all 8 categories.
column2: Alcohol / caffeinated foods and beverages / dairy / high-fat greasy foods / fructose beverages / spicy foods / apples-peaches-pears / sweeteners (sorbitol/mannitol/xylitol/maltitol)

column1: What is moral distress?
column2: When the nurse's actions differ from what they feel is ethically correct.

column1: PTSD manifestations?
column2: Recurring flashbacks / nightmares / sweating / increased heart rate / exaggerated startle response. Symptoms may be delayed and can become chronic.

column1: Self-concept vs self-esteem — what is the difference?
column2: Self-concept = how you THINK about yourself (beliefs/preferences/opinions — a learned behavior). Self-esteem = how you FEEL about yourself.

column1: Kübler-Ross 5 stages
column2: Denial → Anger → Bargaining → Depression → Acceptance. NOT sequential — patients can move back and forth between stages.

column1: Bereavement vs mourning — what is the difference?
column2: Bereavement = the PERIOD OF TIME during which a person experiences grief and mourning. Mourning = the OUTWARD PUBLIC expression of grief.

column1: What are Worden's 4 tasks of grieving?
column2: 1. Accept the reality of the loss 2. Experience the pain and grief 3. Adjust to environment without deceased 4. Find enduring connection while moving forward

column1: What is compassion fatigue and who is at highest risk?
column2: Cumulative stress from wanting to help those suffering but being unable to relieve it → professional uselessness and self-blame. Highest risk: ER / critical care / end-of-life nurses.

column1: What is the most effective communication style and why?
column2: ASSERTIVE — communicates clearly and honestly / advocates for own opinions without violating others' rights. Fundamental to good communication and mental health.

column1: Passive vs passive-aggressive communication — what is the difference?
column2: Passive = avoids conflict / agrees to prevent confrontation / anxious. Passive-aggressive = appears passive on surface but acts out anger subtly / sarcasm / stems from powerlessness and resentment.

column1: Therapeutic communication techniques — name them all.
column2: Silence / Active listening / Open-ended questions / Accepting / Restating and summarizing / Reflecting

column1: Nontherapeutic communication — what to avoid?
column2: Giving advice / not listening / false reassurance / rejecting what patient says / being critical / not addressing patient's concerns

column1: What is motivational interviewing (OARS)?
column2: Open-ended questions / Affirmations / Reflective listening / Summarizing. Used to help clients develop plans to promote their own health.

column1: Language barrier — what must the nurse do?
column2: Use a CERTIFIED MEDICAL INTERPRETER — NEVER use family members (risk for errors due to lack of medical terminology knowledge).

column1: How should you communicate with a hearing-impaired patient?
column2: Speak in a LOWER register (not louder) / FACE the patient directly.

column1: Which learning domain involves hands-on physical skills?
column2: Psychomotor — physical movement, skills, coordination, and use of the senses.

column1: What does a Respiratory Therapist do?
column2: Manages oxygen and oxygenation devices / manages ventilator settings / gives respiratory treatments.

column1: What does a Speech Therapist treat?
column2: Communication/speaking impairments AND swallowing disorders.

column1: What is the role of Assistive Personnel (AP/UAP)?
column2: Nurses' aides who assist the healthcare team. Clinical reasoning CANNOT be delegated to AP.

column1: Presbycusis vs presbyopia — what is the difference?
column2: Presbycusis = loss of hearing SIBILANT sounds (Sh/Ph/S/Ch) and high-pitched sounds. Presbyopia = becoming more FARSIGHTED with aging.

column1: GI changes in older adults?
column2: Gag reflex is diminished / peristalsis decreases (constipation risk) / external sphincter control weakens (incontinence risk).

column1: What is osteoporosis and who is at highest risk?
column2: Bones become porous and susceptible to fracture. Highest risk = post-menopausal women. Weight-bearing exercise is essential to preserve bone density.

column1: Osteoporosis risk factors?
column2: Insufficient calcium and Vitamin D / decreased estrogen or testosterone / prolonged bed rest / seizure medications or hormone treatments / eating disorder history / excessive alcohol / smoking / family history

column1: What is Alzheimer's disease and what are the first signs?
column2: Progressive irreversible brain disorder destroying memory and thinking skills. First signs = mild memory problems. Progresses to confusion / communication difficulties / personality changes / incontinence / loss of mobility / fully dependent.

column1: Recommended vaccines for older adults?
column2: Influenza annually / Shingles (herpes zoster) vaccine at age 50+ / Pneumococcal (PPSV23) at age 65+

column1: Cultural awareness vs cultural competence — what is the difference?
column2: Cultural awareness = ability and willingness to UNDERSTAND differences between cultures. Cultural competence = APPRECIATING / ACCEPTING / RESPECTING individual cultural beliefs — goes beyond just understanding.

column1: Emic vs etic knowledge — what is the difference?
column2: Emic = cultural INSIDER's perspective. Etic = cultural OUTSIDER's perspective. Integrating both leads to cultural competence.

column1: Who is Madeleine Leininger and what did she discover?
column2: Founder of Transcultural Nursing Theory. Discovered nurses need better understanding of patients' cultures. Patients are more likely to follow recommendations when caregivers respect their cultural norms.

column1: Complementary vs alternative therapy — what is the difference?
column2: Complementary = done IN CONJUNCTION with prescribed treatment. Alternative = done INSTEAD OF prescribed treatment.

column1: What are the nursing implications for CAM?
column2: Include CAM in assessment / encourage patient to tell provider before starting herbals / do NOT judge or show disapproval (patient may not share again) / natural does NOT mean safe (ricin and botulism are natural).

column1: Is the incident report part of the medical record?
column2: NO — it is a risk management tool. NEVER reference it in the medical chart. Document separately in the medical record.

column1: What is falsification of health records?
column2: Documenting inaccurate / incomplete / or misleading data OR documenting care that did not actually occur. Examples: not documenting an assessment / documenting care you did not do.

column1: Primary vs secondary vs tertiary prevention — what is each?
column2: Primary = prevent disease BEFORE it occurs (immunizations/health teaching). Secondary = early detection (screenings/mammograms). Tertiary = reduce impact of established disease / minimize disability (cardiac rehab/diabetes management).

column1: What is health literacy?
column2: The capacity to obtain, communicate, and understand basic health information and services to make appropriate health decisions.

column1: What is Healthy People 2030?
column2: 10-year national health objectives updated every 10 years. Goals include: decrease infant mortality / improve life expectancy / decrease obesity.

column1: What are the 4 NLN integrating competencies?
column2: Human flourishing / Nursing judgment / Professional identity / Spirit of inquiry

column1: What is the nursing shortage caused by?
column2: Large number of nurses retiring by 2030 / increased chronic illness patients / limited nursing faculty / increased number of people over 65

column1: What is Naloxone (Narcan)?
column2: The antidote for opioids.

column1: What are the benefits of an interprofessional team?
column2: Improved access and coordination of care / greater referral efficiency / increased quality of community health services / decreased complications / decreased length of stay / decreased mortality and staff turnover

column1: What is a consult vs a referral vs a transfer of care?
column2: Consult = one provider requests another's input or advice. Referral = provider delegates management of a condition to another provider. Transfer of care = systematically turn care over to another provider.

column1: What are silos in healthcare and why are they dangerous?
column2: Groups within an organization that work only within their own area — creates barriers to communication and fragmented care that can negatively impact patient safety.

column1: What is cognitive rehearsal?
column2: Visualizing a difficult or anxiety-producing scenario ahead of time to prepare constructive responses when it arises in real life.

column1: What are the 6 steps of clinical judgment (NCLEX framework)?
column2: 1. Recognize cues 2. Analyze cues 3. Prioritize hypotheses 4. Generate solutions 5. Take actions 6. Evaluate outcomes

column1: What is missed nursing care?
column2: Care that is left undone / omitted / or missed due to limited resources. Considered a medical error that can affect patient safety.

column1: What are the Maslow physiological needs (bottom level)?
column2: Food / water / air / shelter / sleep / clothing / reproduction — must be met before any other needs.

column1: What causes airway obstruction?
column2: CNS depression / blockages from blood or vomit / edema and inflammation of upper airway / facial trauma / foreign objects inside airway

column1: How is adequacy of CIRCULATION assessed in ABCDE?
column2: Blood pressure / capillary refill time / pulse rate-volume-character / urine output / level of consciousness / skin tone changes

column1: What does Disability assess in ABCDE?
column2: Neurologic status — level of consciousness / response to verbal or painful stimulation / level of orientation

column1: What are the elements of informed consent (list all)?
column2: Proposed treatment or procedure / who will perform it / purpose / expected outcomes / benefits / risks / alternatives / benefits and risks of alternatives / client's right to refuse

column1: What is a sentinel event?
column2: An occurrence resulting in permanent disability / temporary severe injury / or death of a client.

column1: What are the ANA 6 social media principles?
column2: 1. Never post identifiable client info 2. Maintain professional boundaries 3. Assume anything posted can be seen by clients/peers/supervisors 4. Use privacy settings 5. Advocate for client rights / report violations 6. Work with employer on policies

column1: Which state is the only one with a law limiting client-to-nurse ratios?
column2: California

column1: What is nurse fatigue?
column2: Physical and psychological exhaustion that causes the nurse to be unable to function safely and competently. Nurses working long hours have higher risk of chronic illness and errors.

column1: What is the 5 rights of delegation — right circumstance specifically?
column2: The client's condition must be STABLE. The delegatee must communicate any changes in the client's condition to the nurse.

column1: What is the purpose of the C (Contain) in RACE?
column2: Closing doors and windows decreases the oxygen supply to the fire — slowing its spread.

column1: NPSGs — what is the universal protocol for surgery?
column2: 2 identifiers → mark the surgical site → perform a time-out before the procedure to confirm correct client / correct site / and correct procedure.

column1: NPSGs — what does "use medications safely" require?
column2: Label all medications / extra caution with anticoagulants (warfarin/heparin) / medication reconciliation at admission-discharge-transfer

column1: NPSGs — what does the suicide risk goal require?
column2: Screen all patients 12+ admitted for behavioral health using a validated tool / remove harmful items from room / round-the-clock surveillance for at-risk clients

column1: What are the 6 Braden Scale categories?
column2: Sensory perception / Moisture / Activity / Mobility / Nutrition / Friction and shear

column1: What is wound dehiscence?
column2: Wound edges separate — the wound reopens.

column1: What is the nursing intervention frequency for repositioning?
column2: Every 2 hours minimum to prevent pressure injuries.

column1: What is cancer pain?
column2: A recognized category of pain including tumor pain / bone pain / and treatment-associated pain (chronic post-surgical pain / chemo effects).

column1: What is a Nonverbal Pain Scale used for?
column2: For clients who cannot verbalize pain — originally developed for burn units / now used in critical care for sedated or ventilated patients.

column1: Cutaneous stimulation for pain — what are examples?
column2: Heat / cold / touch / massage / acupuncture / acupressure / TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation)

column1: Cognitive strategies for pain — what are examples?
column2: Distraction / relaxation / guided imagery / music therapy. Do NOT require a provider prescription — nurses can implement independently.

column1: Sleep hours by age — fill in: newborns / infants / toddlers / school-age / adolescents?
column2: Newborns = 14-17 hrs / Infants = 12-15 hrs / Toddlers = 11-14 hrs / School-age = 9-11 hrs / Adolescents = 8-10 hrs

column1: What is hypersomnia?
column2: Excessive daytime fatigue NOT improved by more sleep. Poor memory / depression / short attention span / irritability. Cause often unknown.

column1: What is restless leg syndrome (Willis-Ekbom disease)?
column2: Uncontrollable urge to move legs with uncomfortable sensation. Symptoms worsen in evening and at bedtime. Avoid caffeine / nicotine / alcohol. Can occur with iron or vitamin deficiencies.

column1: What promotes sleep (key interventions)?
column2: Avoid caffeine/alcohol/nicotine 4-6 hours before bed / dark quiet cool room / consistent sleep schedule / naps under 30 minutes / exercise at least 3 hours before bed

column1: Contraindications to massage therapy?
column2: Burns / wounds / patients on blood thinners (warfarin)

column1: What is the cardiovascular diet sodium limit?
column2: Decrease sodium intake — limit to reduce hypertension and heart disease risk.

column1: What does a post-surgery diet focus on and why?
column2: Increase PROTEIN — needed to repair tissues and aid healing after surgery.

column1: What is a soft diet used for?
column2: Soft / low-fiber / easy-to-digest foods. May be prescribed long-term for clients with dysphagia.

column1: What is a regular diet?
column2: No dietary restrictions — consists of healthy foods from all food groups.

column1: Why should you NEVER lower the HOB to flat during a tube feeding?
column2: Increases aspiration risk. HOB must stay at 30-45° during tube feedings and for at least 1 hour after bolus feedings.

column1: What are the Mendelsohn maneuver and supraglottic swallow?
column2: Supraglottic swallow = hold breath → swallow → cough to clear residual. Mendelsohn maneuver = hold the swallow for 2-3 seconds then complete it. Both are dysphagia swallowing techniques.

column1: What is functional incontinence and an example?
column2: Physical inability to reach the toilet in time due to physical impairment. Example: wheelchair-bound patient or arthritis of hands limiting ability to unbutton clothing.

column1: Constipation interventions — list all from the wrap-up.
column2: High-fiber diet / adequate fluids / exercise / bowel training / stool softeners / assist to toilet promptly when needed.

column1: What does FOBT stand for and what does it test?
column2: Fecal Occult Blood Test — checks stool for hidden (occult) blood. Test turns BLUE if blood is present.

column1: What are adventitious stressors?
column2: Rare and unexpected events — natural disasters (floods/earthquakes/war), interpersonal disasters (assault), and acts of terrorism.

column1: What is self-concept and what shapes it?
column2: How people perceive or think about themselves — a learned behavior shaped by: life experiences / heredity / cultural attitudes / academic achievement / career / role performance / relationships / health status. Most flexible during early development.

column1: What are the 4 components of self-concept?
column2: Body image (perception of own physical appearance) / Role performance / Personal identity / Self-esteem

column1: What is the dual process model of grief?
column2: Grief oscillates between two stressors: loss-oriented (intense emotions about the loss itself) and restoration-oriented (coping with secondary losses and rebuilding life). Moving between both is healthy.

column1: What are the age-related grief responses for preschoolers vs adolescents?
column2: Preschoolers = view death as temporary and reversible / magical thinking / may believe their thoughts caused the death. Adolescents = full understanding of death / may rely more on peers / may appear dismissive or act out.

column1: What are the 4 phases of a therapeutic relationship?
column2: Orientation (client reaches out) → Identification (establish respectful relationship) → Exploitation (active phase / nurse educates client) → Termination (issue resolved / relationship ends)

column1: Verbal vs nonverbal communication — which takes precedence when they conflict?
column2: NONVERBAL takes precedence — body language often outweighs what is being said verbally.

column1: What are the modes of communication?
column2: Verbal (oral / face-to-face / telephone) / Nonverbal (body language) / Electronic (email/texting/video) / Written (letters/email)

column1: What is the teach-back method?
column2: Asking the client to explain information back in their own words to verify understanding.

column1: Who requires client education per the Joint Commission?
column2: Client education is a TJC requirement for hospital accreditation. Effectively educated clients have less anxiety / less pain / fewer unpleasant hospital experiences.

column1: What should the nurse assess BEFORE teaching?
column2: Readiness to learn — includes emotional state / physical condition / motivation / health literacy / language / barriers

column1: What does a Social Worker do in healthcare?
column2: Collaborates with the interprofessional team to find solutions to client challenges / advocates for resources / helps resolve issues.

column1: What does a Physical Therapist focus on vs Occupational Therapist?
column2: PT = GROSS motor skills (walking/balance/strength/pain). OT = FINE motor skills (dressing/cooking/writing) and return to daily living and work.

column1: Musculoskeletal changes in older adults?
column2: Loss of bone and muscle mass / joint stiffness / diminished ROM / spinal curvature / postural changes → increased fall risk. Menopausal women lose bone faster → osteoporosis risk.

column1: Cardiovascular changes in older adults?
column2: Heart valves thicken and become more rigid / loss of elasticity in blood vessels / increased hypertension risk / increased susceptibility to cardiac and respiratory disorders.

column1: Integumentary changes in older adults?
column2: Skin loses elasticity / becomes thinner-drier-more fragile / loss of subcutaneous fat / nails become brittle / hair loss common

column1: What is gerontology?
column2: The multidisciplinary study of aging across the lifespan.

column1: What is a cultural health assessment?
column2: A type of data collection to gather information about the client's culture and how it affects their health.

column1: What is Leininger's Sunrise Enabler?
column2: A visual tool to help nurses provide culturally congruent care by considering all cultural factors that influence a client's health and well-being.

column1: Health disparities — what are social determinants of health?
column2: Factors that influence health outcomes: economic stability / education / social context / healthcare access / neighborhood and environment

column1: What is the nurse's responsibility regarding herbal supplements?
column2: Include ALL supplements in nursing assessment / list alongside medications / encourage patient to disclose to provider / do not judge. Herbals and vitamins are regulated as FOOD not medicine.

column1: Complementary vs alternative vs integrative therapy?
column2: Complementary = IN CONJUNCTION with prescribed treatment. Alternative = INSTEAD OF prescribed treatment. Integrative = combines conventional and evidence-based CAM approaches.

column1: What are the advantages of EHRs (electronic health records)?
column2: Real-time access by all interprofessional team members / reduces errors / built-in clinical alerts / improved coordination / more reliable coding and billing

column1: What are guidelines for accurate documentation?
column2: Must be accurate / complete / factual / and timely. Never falsify records. Document only what actually occurred.

column1: What are examples of falsification of health records?
column2: Not documenting a client assessment / not documenting communication with team / documenting inaccurate assessment data / documenting care that did not actually occur

column1: Primary vs secondary vs tertiary prevention — an example of each?
column2: Primary = immunizations / health teaching (before disease). Secondary = mammograms / blood pressure screenings (early detection). Tertiary = cardiac rehab / diabetes management (after disease established).

column1: What is the WHO definition of health promotion?
column2: A way to empower people to control and improve their physical and mental health. Focus = create access to healthy options and address imbalances from social injustice / poverty / racial injustice / lack of resources.

column1: What are levels of prevention in order?
column2: Primary (prevent disease before it occurs) → Secondary (early detection and treatment) → Tertiary (reduce impact of established disease / minimize disability)

column1: Dysphagia — what are the positioning rules during meals?
column2: HOB at 90° (sit fully upright) / chin tuck while swallowing / follow bites with liquids

column1: Dysphagia — what are the preparation interventions before feeding?
column2: Toilet patient first / remove clutter / dentures if needed / hearing aids if needed / encourage self-feeding / use assistive devices

column1: Dysphagia — what do you monitor for during feeding?
column2: Check for pocketing of food in cheeks / thicken liquids as ordered / monitor for coughing (early sign of aspiration)

column1: What does a clear liquid diet include?
column2: Broth / water / gelatin / clear liquids only. Avoid red coloring for colon procedures and tonsillectomies.

column1: What does a full liquid diet include?
column2: Everything in clear liquid PLUS ice cream / yogurt / pudding / milkshakes / strained soups / protein shakes / gelatin.

column1: What does a pureed diet include?
column2: Smooth foods requiring no chewing — yogurt / pudding / mashed potatoes / pureed meats / broths / ice cream / juices without pulp / baby food

column1: Physiological stress response — cardiovascular and metabolic changes?
column2: Increased BP / increased heart rate / increased blood sugar

column1: Physiological stress response — respiratory and neurological changes?
column2: Increased oxygen consumption (tachypnea / bronchial tubes dilate) / pupil dilation / increased alertness

column1: Hendrich II: Male gender + benzodiazepine + dizziness = how many criteria?
column2: 3 criteria.

column1: Hendrich II: Symptomatic depression + urinary urgency + antiepileptic = how many criteria?
column2: 3 criteria.

column1: What does the Get-Up-and-Go Test assess and which risk tool includes it?
column2: Assesses ability to rise from a chair and walk — one of the 8 criteria of the Hendrich II Fall Risk Model.

column1: What is the Denial stage of grief?
column2: Refuses to believe reality to lessen pain. Often feels numb and shocked. Can include seeking second opinions.

column1: What is the Anger stage of grief?
column2: Blames others and directs hostility at loved ones and caregivers as a way of releasing emotional discomfort.

column1: What is the Bargaining stage of grief?
column2: Negotiates with a higher power in exchange for a different outcome. Guilt is common.

column1: What is the Depression stage of grief?
column2: Reality sets in — profound sadness, withdrawal. Natural and appropriate response to loss.

column1: What is the Acceptance stage of grief?
column2: Still feels pain but believes all will eventually be well. Does not mean happiness.

column1: A 4-year-old cannot verbally rate their pain. Which pain scale should the nurse use?
column2: FLACC Scale — observational tool for children 2 months to 7 years and cognitively disabled patients.

column1: What is the CRIES pain scale and who is it used for?
column2: Observational pain scale for infants born at 38 weeks gestation or greater.

column1: What is the primary goal of shared governance?
column2: To move nurses from the point of care to the decision-making table — giving nurses control over their own practice.

column1: What are the most significant clinical outcomes of shared governance?
column2: Improved client outcomes / better work environments / higher job satisfaction.

column1: What is overt aspiration?
column2: Visible symptoms: cough, wheezing, trouble breathing, fever, congestion, throat clearing, or chest discomfort.

column1: What is silent aspiration?
column2: No obvious symptoms — detected only by vital sign changes (decreased SpO₂, increased HR, BP, RR, or fever ≥38°C).

column1: Do physical restraints reduce falls?
column2: NO — restraints do not reduce falls. They cause physical harm (pressure ulcers / nerve damage / contractures) and emotional harm (anger / fear / humiliation).

column1: What is the ANA standard of care regarding restraints?
column2: Restraint-free environment is the standard. Restraints are a last resort and never resolve the underlying problem.

column1: What is assault in nursing/legal terms?
column2: Making a client feel fearful of harm or offensive contact. Physical contact is NOT required. Example: threatening a patient with restraints.

column1: What is battery in nursing/legal terms?
column2: An act that results in actual harm or injury to a client (illegal restraint, inappropriate touch, wrong-site surgery). Usually treated as a criminal offense.

column1: What is informed consent?
column2: Voluntary permission to receive care after the client is made aware of risks and benefits — given without coercion.

column1: What is implied consent?
column2: Assumed when a patient cannot consent and delay would pose increased risk to life. Example: unconscious patient in the ED.

column1: When is an NG tube used?
column2: Short-term nutritional support when the stomach is functioning normally. Placed by nurses at the bedside.

column1: When is an NJ tube used?
column2: Short-term nutritional support when the stomach CANNOT tolerate feeding. Bypasses the stomach and delivers to the jejunum.

column1: When is a G-tube used?
column2: Long-term or permanent nutritional support, placed surgically, regardless of the reason.

column1: What is a living will?
column2: A document where a patient states which life-sustaining treatments they want or do not want if they become incapacitated.

column1: What is a durable power of attorney for healthcare?
column2: A document where a patient appoints someone to make healthcare decisions on their behalf if they are unable to.

column1: What is the cognitive learning domain?
column2: The thinking domain — knowledge, understanding, and recall. Example: explaining why a medication is taken.

column1: What is the psychomotor learning domain?
column2: The action domain — physical movement, skills, coordination, and use of the senses. Example: teaching a patient to self-inject insulin.

column1: What is the affective learning domain?
column2: The emotional domain — feelings, attitudes, and values. Must be addressed before cognitive or psychomotor learning can occur.

column1: A cognitively disabled adult cannot verbalize pain. Which observational pain scale is used?
column2: FLACC Scale — used for children 2 months to 7 years AND cognitively disabled patients of any age.

column1: A neonate born at 40 weeks is post-surgical and cannot verbalize pain. Which pain scale is used?
column2: CRIES Scale — observational scale for infants born at 38 weeks gestation or greater.

column1: What does a Physical Therapist (PT) do?
column2: Works on gross motor skills — walking, balance, strength, and movement. Helps improve mobility and alleviate pain.

column1: What does an Occupational Therapist (OT) do?
column2: Works on fine motor skills and daily living activities — dressing, cooking, writing, returning to work.

column1: What are examples of physical restraints?
column2: Ties, straps, vests, and mitts. Casts, traction, and holding for a procedure are NOT restraints.

column1: What are chemical restraints?
column2: Medications used to sedate or control behavior (benzodiazepines, antipsychotics). Require a provider order.

column1: Where must the Foley catheter drainage bag always be positioned?
column2: Below the level of the bladder at all times — never on the floor, never above the bladder.

column1: How is a Foley catheter secured to prevent tension on the urethra?
column2: Taped to the patient's leg.

column1: Why must a Foley catheter maintain a closed drainage system?
column2: Breaking the closed system introduces bacteria and increases risk of CAUTI (catheter-associated UTI).

column1: How often should the urinary meatus be cleaned in a patient with a Foley catheter?
column2: At least once daily with soap and water — more often if soiled.

column1: What is Acute Stress Disorder (ASD)?
column2: An intense, dysfunctional reaction to trauma with symptoms lasting LESS than one month.

column1: What is PTSD?
column2: A prolonged stress reaction to trauma with symptoms lasting MORE than one month. Symptoms can be delayed and may become chronic.

column1: When is TPN used?
column2: When the GI tract cannot absorb or tolerate adequate nutrition. Nutrition is delivered intravenously into a large vein.

column1: When is a G-tube used vs an NG tube?
column2: G-tube = long-term or permanent. NG tube = short-term with functioning stomach. Key difference: duration of need.

column1: When is an NG tube used vs a G-tube?
column2: NG tube = short-term, placed by nurses. G-tube = long-term or permanent, placed surgically.

column1: When is an NJ tube used vs an NG tube?
column2: NJ tube = short-term when stomach CANNOT tolerate feeding. NG tube = short-term when stomach IS functioning.

column1: What defines a Stage 3 pressure injury?
column2: Full-thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat may be visible but NO bone, tendon, or muscle is exposed.

column1: What defines a Stage 4 pressure injury?
column2: Full-thickness skin AND tissue loss with bone, tendon, or muscle exposed or directly palpable.

column1: On the Braden Scale, what does a lower score indicate?
column2: Greater risk for pressure injury. Lower score = greater risk.

column1: What are the 6 categories of the Braden Scale?
column2: Sensory perception / Moisture / Activity / Mobility / Nutrition / Friction and shear

column1: What defines constipation?
column2: Fewer than three bowel movements per week with stools that are hard, lumpy, and difficult to pass.

column1: Which constipation symptoms require immediate medical attention?
column2: Fever / GI bleeding / abdominal pain / vomiting / low back pain / unexplained weight loss.

column1: What is an actual nursing diagnosis?
column2: Problem is happening NOW. Written in PES format: Problem + Etiology + Signs/Symptoms.

column1: What is a risk nursing diagnosis?
column2: Problem has NOT occurred yet. Written as Problem + Risk Factors. No signs/symptoms listed.

column1: What is a health promotion nursing diagnosis?
column2: Patient is ready and motivated to improve their health status. No problem exists — patient wants to enhance wellness.

column1: What is Beneficence?
column2: The nurse's obligation to minimize harm AND actively practice in a way that benefits the client — going above what is required.

column1: What is Nonmaleficence?
column2: The nurse's obligation to do no harm — or the least amount of harm while achieving the best possible outcome.

column1: What does the Good Samaritan Law protect?
column2: Protection from negligence claims when providing care outside employment without expectation of payment. Laws vary by state.

column1: What three things void Good Samaritan protection?
column2: Receiving compensation / being negligent / practicing outside scope of practice.

column1: What are the most dangerous opioid side effects to monitor?
column2: Respiratory depression and orthostatic hypotension. Monitor respiratory rate and blood pressure.

column1: What are the common opioid side effects?
column2: Sedation / constipation / nausea and vomiting / itching / rashes / flushing.

column1: Which vitamins are fat-soluble and what do they need to be absorbed?
column2: A, D, E, K — fat must be present in the diet to absorb them.

column1: Which vitamins are water-soluble and how are they different from fat-soluble?
column2: C and B complex — not stored in the body, must be replaced regularly through diet.

column1: What is anticipatory grief?
column2: Grief experienced BEFORE an expected loss — when a loss is anticipated (e.g. terminal diagnosis).

column1: What is disenfranchised grief?
column2: Grief for a loss not recognized by society as worthy of grief. The person grieves alone. Examples: pet loss, miscarriage, suicide loss.

column1: What is a socioeconomic stressor? Give an example.
column2: Stress from poverty, low SES, or homelessness. Example: patient cannot afford medications.

column1: What is a cultural stressor? Give an example.
column2: Stress from not culturally fitting in or receiving care that ignores cultural beliefs. Example: healthcare team ignores patient's traditional healing practices.

column1: What is the Denial stage of grief?
column2: Refuses to believe reality to lessen pain. May feel numb or shocked. Example: "The lab must be wrong."

column1: What is the Bargaining stage of grief?
column2: Negotiates with a higher power in exchange for a different outcome. Guilt is common. Example: "If I survive, I promise I will help others."

column1: What is normal grief?
column2: Grief lasting several months to a year that gradually lessens in intensity over time. Experienced differently by everyone.

column1: What is prolonged grief disorder?
column2: Grief lasting longer than 6 months that significantly impairs daily functioning. Marked by inability to accept the death and preoccupation with the deceased.

column1: What is the Anger stage of grief?
column2: Blames others and directs hostility at loved ones and caregivers as a way of releasing emotional discomfort.

column1: What is the Depression stage of grief?
column2: Reality sets in — profound sadness, withdrawal from others, sense of immense loss. Natural and appropriate.

column1: What is EMTALA and why was it enacted?
column2: Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act — enacted to stop patient dumping. Every ED patient must receive a Medical Screening Exam regardless of ability to pay.

column1: Under EMTALA, what must happen before a patient is transferred?
column2: The hospital must stabilize the patient first. If unable to stabilize, the physician must sign off that benefits of transfer outweigh the risks.

column1: Licensure by endorsement vs compact license — what is the difference?
column2: Endorsement = applying to practice in another state. Compact license = automatically licensed in all compact states under one multistate license.

column1: What is a situational stressor?
column2: Stress created by personal, family, or work-related issues (job loss, chronic illness, financial strain, death of a family member).

column1: What is a developmental stressor?
column2: Stress that occurs as an individual moves through the stages of life (retirement, marriage, parenthood, aging).

column1: What is an adventitious stressor?
column2: Rare and unexpected disaster events — natural disasters, physical or sexual assault, acts of terrorism.

column1: What is a socioeconomic stressor?
column2: Stress from poverty, low socioeconomic status (SES), or homelessness.

column1: What is a cultural stressor?
column2: Stress from living in a society where one does not culturally fit and/or receiving care that ignores cultural beliefs.

column1: Why are straws contraindicated for patients with dysphagia?
column2: Straws increase aspiration risk by sending liquid too quickly to the back of the throat before the swallow reflex can activate.

column1: What does CRIES stand for?
column2: C — Crying / R — Requires O₂ for saturation >95% / I — Increased vital signs (HR and BP) / E — Expression (facial grimace) / S — Sleepless
